key_concept: Friedel–Crafts acylation converts benzene to acetophenone, a methyl ketone, which undergoes the haloform reaction with $NaOCl$ to give sodium benzoate and chloroform.
steps: Step (i), Friedel–Crafts acylation: $C_6H_6 + CH_3COCl \xrightarrow{AlCl_3} C_6H_5COCH_3 + HCl$. The product is acetophenone, a methyl ketone.

Step (ii), haloform reaction: a $CH_3CO-$ group reacts with $NaOCl$. It gives the sodium salt of the acid with one carbon less, plus haloform: $C_6H_5COCH_3 + 3NaOCl \rightarrow C_6H_5COCCl_3 + 3NaOH$, then $C_6H_5COCCl_3 + NaOH \rightarrow C_6H_5COONa + CHCl_3$.
Statement (1): $P$ is indeed a carboxylate salt, but $Q$ is $CHCl_3$, not a primary alcohol. False.
Statement (2): $P$ is aromatic, but $CHCl_3$ is not. False.

Statement (3): $P$ gives benzoic acid on acidification, $C_6H_5COONa + HCl \rightarrow C_6H_5COOH + NaCl$. $Q$ is slowly oxidised by air in light to poisonous phosgene: $2CHCl_3 + O_2 \xrightarrow{h\nu} 2COCl_2 + 2HCl$. True.
Statement (4): neither sodium benzoate nor chloroform is an aldehyde or ketone. False.
final_answer: Option (3): If P gives a carboxylic acid on acidification, Q gives a poisonous gas on exposure to air and light.
why_not_others: Options (1), (2) and (4) all fail because $Q$ is chloroform. It is not an alcohol, not aromatic and not a carbonyl compound, so only $P$ fits the first part of those statements.
common_trap: Students confuse the haloform reaction with the Cannizzaro reaction. They then assume an alcohol plus a carboxylate salt form, but acetophenone has α-hydrogens and gives $CHCl_3$, not an alcohol.
time_saving_tip: Spot the pattern 'methyl ketone + $NaOX$', which always gives $RCOONa + CHX_3$. Then recall that chloroform forms phosgene in air and light, which is why it is stored in dark bottles filled to the brim.
